The '''Marshall Scholarship''' is a [[Postgraduate student|postgraduate]] [[scholarship]] for "intellectually distinguished young Americans [and] their country's future leaders" to study at any university in the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name=":5">{{cite web |title=United States no. 2 (1953). Proposed arrangements for the administration of the marshall scholarship scheme |url=https://www.marshallscholarship.org/media/1248/1953actofparliamentwithadminregs.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://www.marshallscholarship.org/media/ |archive-date=May 1, 1953 |publisher=Marshall Scholarships}}</ref> It is considered among the most prestigious scholarships for U.S. citizens, and along with the [[Fulbright Scholarship]], it is the only broadly available scholarship available to Americans to study at any university in the United Kingdom.<ref name="nytimes.com">{{cite news |last=Ivry |first=Sara |date=January 12, 2003 |title=Other Roads |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/01/12/education/other-roads.html |access-date=July 23, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=January 26, 2011 |title=10 Most Prestigious Scholarships In America |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/10-most-prestigious-scholarships-in-america/ |website=[[CBS News]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=December 15, 1996 |title=Ambassador Names Marshall Scholars |pages=54 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/12/15/nyregion/ambassador-names-marshall-scholars.html |access-date=July 23, 2022}}</ref>

Created by the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]] in 1953 as a living gift to the [[United States]] in recognition of the generosity of [[United States Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[George C. Marshall]] and the [[Marshall Plan]] in the wake of [[World War II]], the goal of the scholarship was to strengthen the [[Special Relationship]] between the two countries for "the good of mankind in this turbulent world".<ref name=":3">{{cite web|url=http://www.marshallscholarship.org/about/history|title=Message from General George Marshall|website=www.marshallscholarship.org}}</ref> The scholarships are awarded by the [[Marshall Aid Commemoration Commission]] and are largely funded by the [[Government of the United Kingdom|British government]].<ref name="63rd annual report">{{cite book|title=Marshall Aid Commemoration Commission / Year ending 30 September 2016 / 63rd Annual Report|date=March 2017|publisher=Marshall Aid Commemoration Commission|isbn=978-1-4741-4013-3|url=http://www.marshallscholarship.org/about/63rd_annual_report|access-date=June 16, 2017}}</ref> The program was also the first major co-educational British graduate scholarship; one-third of the inaugural cohort in 1954 were women. With nearly 1,000 university-endorsed applicants in recent years—along with many more who apply but do not receive their university's endorsement—the Marshall Scholarship ranks among the most selective graduate scholarships for Americans. Among university-endorsed applicants, the acceptance rate typically ranges from three to four percent, reaching as low as 3.2 percent in 2015 and 3.6 percent for the 2025 class.<ref name="marshallscholarship2015">{{cite web |date= |title=Annual Reports |url=http://www.marshallscholarship.org/the-commission/annual-reports |access-date=May 30, 2019 |website=Marshall Scholarships}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Nietzel |first=Michael T. |title=Thirty-Six American Students Named Marshall Scholars For 2025 |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2024/12/16/thirty-six-american-students-named-marshall-scholars-for-2025/ |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>

There are more than 1,900 [[#Marshall Scholars|Marshall Scholar alumni]].<ref name="marshallscholarship2015" /> Many of these alumni have achieved distinctions and hold prestigious careers. In the U.S. government, current alumni include an associate justice of the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], members of [[United States Congress|Congress]] and [[Cabinet of the United States|presidential cabinets]], and state [[Governor (United States)|governors]]. Alumni are CEOs of companies such as [[LinkedIn]] and [[Dolby Labs]], and managing editors of [[TIME|''Time'' magazine]] and [[CNN]]. They are also deans of [[Yale Law School]], [[Stanford Law School]], the [[John F. Kennedy School of Government|Harvard Kennedy School]], and [[Harvard College]]; and presidents of [[Duke University]], [[Wellesley College]], the [[Cooper Union]], and [[Caltech]]. They also include two [[Nobel Laureate|Nobel Laureates]], a winner of the [[Kluge Prize]], six [[Pulitzer Prize]]–winning authors, fourteen [[MacArthur Genius Grant]] awardees, [[Anne McClain|NASA's youngest astronaut]], two [[Academy Award|Oscar]] nominees, and [[Kim Campbell (pilot)|one awardee]] of the [[Distinguished Flying Cross (United States)|Distinguished Flying Cross]] for service during the [[Iraq War]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alumni - Marshall Scholarships |url=https://www.marshallscholarship.org/alumni |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=www.marshallscholarship.org |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Marshall Scholar Alumni by Year from Association of Marshall Scholars |url=https://marshallscholars.org/alumni-by-year |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=Association of Marshall Scholars |language=en-US}}</ref>

== History ==
[[File:George Catlett Marshall, general of the US army.jpg|thumb|[[George C. Marshall]], for whom the scholarships are named]]

=== Founding and motivation ===
Plans to establish Marshall Scholarships as a living memorial to [[United States Secretary of State|United States secretary of state]] [[George C. Marshall]] was announced by [[Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)|British Foreign Secretary]] [[Anthony Eden]] on 31 July 1952. They were enacted by the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]] with the [[Marshall Aid Commemoration Act 1953]].<ref>''Britain to Set Up 12 Scholarships for U.S. Students''. The Washington Post, August 1, 1952.</ref>

The authors of the proposal initially considered partnering with the [[Rhodes Scholarship]] and even considered using the same selection committees. This idea was eventually disregarded because its proponents strongly believed the scholarships should be available to women and to married men under the age of 28. At the time, the Rhodes Scholarship was limited to single men under the age of 25 and would remain such for two decades when, following the passage of the British Sex Discrimination Act in 1975, the Rhodes Scholarship became open to women beginning in 1977.<ref name="nytimes.com"/> 

The creation of a separate scholarship was a cause of great concern to Lord [[Godfrey Elton]], the head of the [[Rhodes Trust]] in 1952, who worried that the ability to study at other universities would draw potential applicants. He urged the [[Foreign and Commonwealth Office|Foreign Office]] to create a "reverse exchange" for British students to study in the United States instead.<ref>{{cite book | last=Mukharji | first=Aroop | title=Diplomas and Diplomacy | publisher=Springer | date=2016-05-30 | isbn=978-1-137-58653-7 | pages = 31–32}}</ref> 

In 1959, when Parliament doubled the number of Marshall scholars from 12 to 24, British politician [[Philip Noel-Baker]] argued that "Marshall, more than perhaps any other man, destroyed isolation in the United States and built up the conception that only collective security through international institutions can save the world... I think the world has never seen an act of greater national generosity than Marshall aid and the other aid which the United States has given to other continents throughout the last 15 years". By 1960, six years after its establishment, the scholarship was "on its way to becoming as well-known and respected as the fellow phrase, 'Rhodes [Scholarship]'", and both scholarships attracted roughly 500 to 600 applicants.<ref>Stanford, Neal. ''Marshall Scholars: Terms Compared''. The Christian Science Monitor, January 18, 1960.</ref>

As part of the celebrations for the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Marshall Scholarships in 2003, a [[Marshall Medal]] was awarded to distinguished Americans in recognition of their contributions to UK-US relations, including [[Stephen Breyer]] (1959 Marshall Scholar), [[Ray Dolby]] (1957 Marshall Scholar), [[Thomas L. Friedman]] (1975 Marshall Scholar), and [[Nannerl Keohane]] (1961 Marshall Scholar).<ref>{{cite web |title=HRH presents Marshall Medals at Senate House, London |url=http://www.princeofwales.gov.uk/news-and-diary/hrh-presents-marshall-medals-senate-house-london |website=Prince of Wales}}</ref>

In the early years of the Marshall Scholarship, it was common for new scholars to travel together to the UK on an [[ocean liner]], but later, scholars usually are flown together to London from [[Washington, D.C.]] following a welcome program at the [[White House]] with top United Kingdom and United States government and diplomatic officials. 

=== Evolution ===
In 1954, the first year Marshall Scholarships were awarded, 700 students applied, 74 were interviewed, and 12 were ultimately selected (eight men and four women). Two came from Stanford and the rest from Harvard, Princeton, Dartmouth, Bowdoin, Bryn Mawr, Oberlin, and the state universities of Kentucky, Utah, Virginia, and Wisconsin.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our history - Marshall Scholarships |url=https://www.marshallscholarship.org/about/our-history |access-date=2024-12-23 |website=www.marshallscholarship.org |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 1956, [[Claremont McKenna College|Claremont McKenna]] student [[Hugh Gallagher (advocate)|Hugh Gallagher]] became the first wheelchair user to be selected as a Marshall Scholar. He used the scholarship to study at [[University of Oxford|Oxford]]. He went on to draft the [[Architectural Barriers Act of 1968]], which required that buildings built with federal funds be made accessible to all and the law was enacted by [[Lyndon B. Johnson|President Lyndon B. Johnson]]. This was a precursor to the [[Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990|Americans With Disabilities Act of 1990]]. "Hugh's most outstanding contribution to the quality of life of people with disabilities was to successfully place disability rights on Congress' agenda for the first time", former Senate majority leader [[Bob Dole]] wrote for an event honoring Gallagher in 1995.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Hugh Gallagher Dies: Crusaded for Disabled |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2004/07/16/hugh-gallagher-dies/85d24496-db8b-4669-a244-7b362acec759/ |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

In 1963, [[Boston University]] graduate student John Willis became the first African American to be selected for a Marshall Scholarship. He used the scholarship to study at the [[SOAS University of London|School of Oriental and African Studies]].<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2000 |title=The First Black Marshall Scholar |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2678972 |journal=The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education |issue=27 |pages=19 |jstor=2678972 |issn=1077-3711}}</ref> Willis went on to being a professor emeritus of Near Eastern studies at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Willis, professor emeritus of Near Eastern studies, dies - 12/17/2007 - Princeton Weekly Bulletin |url=https://pr.princeton.edu/pwb/07/1217/willis/ |access-date=2024-12-23 |website=pr.princeton.edu}}</ref>

The number of scholars increased to thirty in 1973, forty in 1991, and 44 between 2004 and 2007. In 2010, the commission decided to offer a limited number of one-year awards.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013 |title=Marshall Scholarships: Corporate Plan 2013-2016 |url=http://www.marshallscholarship.org/about/corporateplan2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150122225901/http://www.marshallscholarship.org/about/corporateplan2014 |archive-date=January 22, 2015 |access-date=January 22, 2015 |website=Marshall Scholarship |publisher=Marshall Aid Commemoration Commission}}</ref> In 2016, the Foreign Office announced that forty scholars had been selected, a 25 percent increase more than the originally planned 32, with Foreign Office Minister [[Alok Sharma]] calling it a demonstration of how "resolute Britain is in its commitment to the special relationship".<ref>{{cite web |title=UK announces more scholarships for US students to strengthen links with USA |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-announces-more-scholarships-for-us-students-to-strengthen-links-with-usa |website=www.gov.uk}}</ref>

On 7 June 2023, British Prime Minister [[Rishi Sunak]], from his office at [[10 Downing Street]], announced an expansion to the funding allotted for Marshall Scholarships, writing in a press release that "the number of Marshall scholarships will increase by 25%, to 50 places a year".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://marshallscholars.org/news-and-updates/prime-minister-announces-marshall-scholarship-increase|title=Prime Minister Announces Increase in Marshall Scholarships and Future Funding|website=Association of Marshall Scholars}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-to-host-first-global-summit-on-artificial-intelligence|title=UK to host first global summit on Artificial Intelligence|date=7 June 2023|website=GOV.UK}}</ref> Accordingly, 51 students were selected as 2024 Marshall Scholars, the largest cohort in the 70-year history of the scholarship,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nietzel |first=Michael T. |title=The Marshall Scholars For 2024 Have Been Announced |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2023/12/11/the-marshall-scholars-for-2024-have-been-announced/ |access-date=2024-12-23 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref> however, only 36 students were selected the next year as 2025 Marshall Scholars.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nietzel |first=Michael T. |title=Thirty-Six American Students Named Marshall Scholars For 2025 |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2024/12/16/thirty-six-american-students-named-marshall-scholars-for-2025/ |access-date=2024-12-23 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>

== Objectives ==
In a letter to the first class of Marshall Scholars, [[George Marshall]] echoed his own words in initially presenting his ideas for European recovery by saying, "A close accord between our two countries is essential to the good of mankind in this turbulent world of today, and that is not possible without an intimate understanding of each other. These scholarships point the way to the continuation and growth of the understanding which found its necessity in the terrible struggle of the war years."<ref name=":3" />

The published objectives of the Marshall Scholarships are outlined as follows:
# "To enable intellectually distinguished young Americans, their country's future leaders, to study in the UK"
# "To help scholars gain an understanding and appreciation of contemporary Britain"
# "To contribute to the advancement of knowledge in science, technology, the humanities and social sciences, and the creative arts at Britain's centres of academic excellence"
# "To motivate scholars to act as ambassadors from the U.S. to the UK and vice versa throughout their lives thus strengthening British American understanding"
# "To promote the personal and academic fulfillment of each scholar"<ref name="auto">{{cite web|title=2024 Rules for candidates wishing to apply for a two year MarshallScholarship|url=https://www.marshallscholarship.org/media/2553/rules-2-year-2024_v3-final.pdf|date=2024}}</ref>

== Selection ==
=== Selection criteria ===
The first proposed arrangement of the Marshall Scholarship, a ten-page 1953 document presented by the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs to Parliament by Command of Her Majesty, instructed selectors to "look for distinction of intellect and character as evidenced both by their scholastic attainment and by other activities and achievements".<ref name=":5" /> It specified:

<blockquote>Preference will be given to candidates who combine high academic ability with the capacity to play an active part in the life of the United Kingdom university to which they go. A Marshall scholar, as the possessor of a keen intellect and a broad outlook, would be thought of as a person who would contribute to the aims General Marshall had in mind when, speaking at Cambridge, Massachusetts, on the 5th of June, 1947 of economic assistance for Europe, he said, "An essential part of any successful action on the part of the United States is an understanding on the part of the American people of the character of the problem and the remedies to be applied. 
Political passion and prejudice should have no part. With foresight and the willingness on the part of our people to face up to the vast responsibilities which history has clearly placed upon our country, the difficulties... can and will be overcome."<ref name=":5" />

</blockquote>Prospective applicants must first be endorsed by their universities to apply. The selection process is then coordinated through the eight major British embassy/consulate regions in the United States ([[Atlanta]], [[Boston]], [[Chicago]], [[Houston]], [[Los Angeles]], [[New York City|New York]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Washington, D.C.]]). Selection committees in each region, consisting of former scholars and other distinguished individuals, receive university-endorsed applications (including personal statements and essays) that are used to select a short list of candidates for interviews. Each committee then interviews each of the regional finalists before making the final decisions on the year's awards. In 2014, sixteen percent of university-endorsed applicants received an interview.<ref name="marshallscholarship2015" />

Although most of the responsibility for selecting the recipients is in the hands of the committees, a few formal guidelines have been outlined in the official selection criteria, most notably:

<blockquote>As future leaders, with a lasting understanding of British society, Marshall Scholars will strengthen the enduring relationship between the British and American peoples, their governments, and their institutions. Marshall Scholars are talented, independent, and wide-ranging in their interests, and their time as Scholars will enhance their intellectual and personal growth. Their direct engagement with Britain through its best academic programmes will contribute to their ultimate personal success. In appointing Scholars the selectors will look for a distinction of intellect and character as evidenced both by their scholastic attainments and by their other activities and achievements. Preference will be given to candidates who display the potential to make a significant contribution to their own society. Selectors will also look for strong motivation and seriousness of purpose, including the presentation of a specific and realistic academic programme.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |date=2021 |title=Who is eligible |url=http://www.marshallscholarship.org/fellowships/eligible |access-date=July 23, 2022 |website=Marshall Scholarships}}</ref></blockquote>

Between 900 and 1000 students typically are endorsed to apply for the Marshall Scholarship annually. In 2015 and 2016, 3.2 and 3.5 percent of university-endorsed applicants to the Marshall Scholarship were elected.<ref name="marshallscholarship2015" /><ref name="jennajohnson">{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=Jenna |date=November 26, 2013 |title=Meet the 2014 Rhodes Scholars |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/education/meet-the-2014-rhodes-scholars/2013/11/26/ea276b1a-5600-11e3-835d-e7173847c7cc_story.html}}</ref> In 2020, 1,000 students were endorsed, 160 interviewed, and 46 selected.<ref name="marshallscholarship2015" />

The Marshall selection committees place a strong emphasis on academic achievement and potential, and as such, the application requires a minimum grade point average of 3.7 GPA. Successful applicants, however, typically have much higher GPAs—more than half of applicants have perfect academic records.<ref>{{cite web|title = The Marshall Scholarship {{!}} Writing Personal Statements Online|url = https://www.e-education.psu.edu/writingpersonalstatementsonline/p5_p7.html|website = www.e-education.psu.edu|access-date = December 26, 2015}}</ref> Winners from [[Harvard University]] have had average GPA of 3.92, and [[Stanford University]] recommends that applicants have a GPA of 3.8 or above.<ref>{{cite web |title=Should I Apply |url=https://icenter.stanford.edu/orc/Handouts/RM_1_Should_I_Apply.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305184144/https://icenter.stanford.edu/orc/Handouts/RM_1_Should_I_Apply.pdf |archive-date=March 5, 2016 |access-date=December 26, 2015 |website=Stanford University |publisher=The Overseas Resource Center}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Harvard Post-Graduate |url=http://cabot.harvard.edu/content/Post-Graduate.docx |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141224142940/http://cabot.harvard.edu/content/Post-Graduate.docx |archive-date=December 24, 2014 |publisher=Harvard}}</ref>

Between 1954 and 2022, 256 of 2,179 the scholars received their undergraduate degrees from [[Harvard University]] (12 percent), 138 from [[Princeton University]], 125 from [[Yale University]], 94 from [[Stanford University]], and 83 from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Among public universities, the top producers are the [[United States Military Academy]], with 47 scholars, followed by the [[United States Naval Academy]] (34 scholars) and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (33 scholars). The following table includes those institutions that have produced 30 or more scholars since 1954.<ref>{{cite web|title = Winners of the 2022 Marshall Scholarship|url = https://www.marshallscholarship.org/the-scholars/winners-of-the-2022-scholarship|website = www.marshallscholarship.org|access-date = September 2, 2022}}</ref><ref name="marshallscholarship2015" />

=== Scholarship terms ===
Marshall Scholars may study any full-time postgraduate course offered by a UK university excluding pre-professional programs, whether a taught master's program, a research degree, or a PhD. The basic tenure of the scholarship is two years. University and college fees are paid by the British government. In addition, scholars receive a quarterly maintenance stipend to cover accommodation and living expenses.<ref name="auto"/>

== Academic destinations ==
Nine institutions are traditionally the main destinations of selected Marshall Scholars: [[University of Oxford]], [[University of Cambridge]], [[London School of Economics]], [[University College London]], [[University of Edinburgh]], [[King's College London]], and [[Imperial College London]].<ref name="marshallscholarship2015" /> Sometimes [[The School of Oriental and African Studies|SOAS]] and the [[London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine]] also have been highly preferred.<ref name="marshallscholarship2015" />

In 2015, there were 69 Marshall Scholars in residence at British universities including those who were selected for the classes of 2012, 2013, and 2014.<ref name=":4" /> During this time, there were 27 scholars at the University of Oxford, seventeen at the [[University of London]] (including five each at the London School of Economics and King's College London, and one at University College London), thirteen at the University of Cambridge, and four at Imperial College London. Of these scholars, 46 were studying arts and social sciences, while 23 were studying science, engineering, or mathematics.<ref name=":4">{{cite web |date=2015 |title=Annual report |url=http://www.marshallscholarship.org/about/62ndannualreportfinal |access-date=May 30, 2019 |website=Marshall Scholarship}}</ref>

== Comparison to other post-graduate scholarships ==
In structure and selection criteria, the Marshall Scholarship is most similar to the American Rhodes Scholarship and the Fulbright Program. Like the Fulbright that is available for study in the United Kingdom, Marshall Scholars may study at any university in the UK. However, under the Fulbright, applicants compete in separate pools for 43 specified universities of varying selectivity, except for two awards tenable at any university.<ref>{{cite web|title = Countries|url = http://us.fulbrightonline.org/countries/selectedcountry/united-kingdom|website = us.fulbrightonline.org|access-date = December 26, 2015|archive-date = September 30, 2020|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200930154203/https://us.fulbrightonline.org/countries/selectedcountry/united-kingdom|url-status = dead}}</ref>

The Marshall Scholarship is more flexible than the Rhodes Scholarship, in that Marshall Scholars may study at any British university and also, may attend a different university each year during a Scholar's tenure.<ref name="nytimes.com" /> In addition, a limited number of one-year Marshall scholarships are available. Unlike Rhodes Scholars, Marshall Scholars must be American citizens (in comparison, approximately eighty Rhodes Scholarships are given annually to citizens of more than a dozen countries). In the process, the Marshall Scholarship is roughly as selective as the Rhodes and [[Mitchell Scholarship]]s: the Marshall was awarded to 3.4 percent of university-endorsed applicants in 2014, compared to 3.7 percent for the Rhodes in 2014, and 3.2 percent for the Mitchell Scholarship in 2017.<ref name="us-irelandalliance.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.us-irelandalliance.org/mitchellscholarship/announcements|title=Announcements {{!}} The Mitchell Scholarship {{!}} US-Ireland Alliance|website=www.us-irelandalliance.org|language=en|access-date=November 18, 2018}}</ref><ref name="jennajohnson" /><ref name="marshallscholarship2015" /> In 2025, the 3.66 percent of university-endorsed applicants received the Marshall, compared to 3.70 percent of university-endorsed applicants for the Rhodes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=3 Harvard College Seniors Named 2025 Marshall Scholars {{!}} News {{!}} The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2024/12/16/marshall-scholarship-2025/ |access-date=2025-01-16 |website=www.thecrimson.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Six Harvard Students Selected as Rhodes Scholars From US, Canada {{!}} News {{!}} The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2024/11/18/rhodes-scholars-announced-harvard-students/ |access-date=2025-01-16 |website=www.thecrimson.com}}</ref> The [[Gates Cambridge Scholarship]] is slightly more selective, with 1.3% of applicants receiving an award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-19 |title=Closing gender gaps for good |url=https://www.gatescambridge.org/about/news/closing-gender-gaps-for-good/ |access-date=2022-02-27 |website=Gates Cambridge |language=en}}</ref> Also, because the selection processes of the scholarships discussed above differ, the likelihood that an applicant will be granted a final round interview is different for each scholarship. In 2014, 15.9 percent of university-endorsed applicants for the Marshall Scholarship received a finalist interview, compared to 24 percent of Rhodes applicants and 5.4 percent of Mitchell applicants.<ref name="us-irelandalliance.org"/><ref name="jennajohnson" /><ref name="marshallscholarship2015" />

While the selection committees continue to emphasize academic potential, over time "the Marshall program has become more Rhodes-like, stating that it is seeking persons who also demonstrate leadership potential". In general, "nearly all Rhodes Scholars are willing to admit that, by and large, the Marshalls are superior if one looks just at grade point averages and other signs of academic achievement", but this is a point of both "admiration" and "disdain".<ref name="Schaeper">Schaeper, Thomas and Kathleen Schaeper. "Rhodes Scholars: Oxford, and the Creation of an American Elite," 2010. Berghahn Books: New York</ref>{{rp|293}} [[Walter Isaacson]], describing Rhodes Scholars as "fairly intelligent, well-rounded, honest people who could be counted on to be upstanding citizens", has said that "the real geniuses... were the Marshall Scholars", perhaps because of the expectation that Rhodes Scholars be "all-rounders". In practice, the Marshall and Rhodes have engaged an "informal rivalry", but in career trajectory after the completion of their fellowships, "the line between [the fellowships] is not so evident", with scholars pursuing similar fields with similar success. In general, a higher percentage of Marshall Scholars "go on to careers in academia and research, whereas Rhodes Scholars are more evenly scattered through the full range of professional occupations".<ref name="Schaeper"/>{{rp|357}}

== Association of Marshall Scholars ==
The Association of Marshall Scholars (AMS) was formed in 1988 as a [[charitable organization]].<ref>{{cite web |title=History and Mission of the Association of Marshall Scholars |url=https://www.marshallscholars.org/about/history/ |access-date=July 23, 2022 |website=Association of Marshall Scholars}}</ref>

The organization has been led by several notable board and advisory members, including [[Kathleen Sullivan (lawyer)|Kathleen Sullivan]], [[Reid Hoffman]], [[Nannerl Keohane]], [[Peter Orszag]], [[Harold Koh]], [[Roger Tsien]], and [[Daniel Yergin]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Leadership |url=https://www.marshallscholars.org/about/leadership/ |access-date=July 23, 2022 |website=Association of Marshall Scholars}}</ref>

The Association of Marshall Scholars releases an annual public opinion poll in partnership with [[Emerson College]] in Boston, Massachusetts. The poll measures perceptions of the United Kingdom by the American public, highlighting major current issues (e.g. Brexit).

=== The Marshall Forum ===
Every year, the Association of Marshall Scholars hosts the Marshall Forum in a different city. It is a high-profile dialogue engaging top American and British leaders about key transatlantic issues.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Marshall Forum |url=https://marshallscholars.org/marshall-forum |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=Association of Marshall Scholars |language=en-US}}</ref> During Forums that take place during anniversaries of the Scholarship or the Marshall Plan, the Marshall Medal typically is awarded to distinguished individuals who have advanced British-American understanding. These have included [[Lisa D. Cook|Lisa Cook]] (1986 Marshall Scholar), [[Madeleine Albright]], and [[Anne Applebaum]] (1986 Marshall Scholar).<ref>{{Cite web |title=The 2024 Marshall Forum {{!}} Chicago, IL {{!}} June 18, 2024 |url=https://marshallscholars.org/forum2024 |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=Association of Marshall Scholars |language=en-US}}</ref>

In partnership with the [[German Marshall Fund]] and the [[British Embassy, Washington]] in 2017, the Association of Marshall Scholars hosted the Harvard Marshall Forum at [[Harvard University]] to mark the seventieth anniversary of the [[Marshall Plan]] and focused on its legacy and effect today. The event featured 30 speakers including [[Madeleine Albright]] as well as two Marshall Scholars, Supreme Court Justices [[Stephen Breyer]] and [[Neil Gorsuch]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Liptak |first1=Adam |date=June 3, 2017 |title=Gorsuch Rejects Doubts Over 'Rule of Law Today' |pages=A17 |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/06/03/us/politics/gorsuch-rejects-doubts-over-rule-of-law-today.html |access-date=July 23, 2022}}</ref>

In 2018, the association partnered with the British Consulate General in San Francisco and the Bechtel International Center at [[Stanford University]] to host a Marshall Forum on Innovation. The Forum focused on the pipeline of scientific invention in fields that are of particular interest to the United States and the United Kingdom, such as biomedicine and genetics. Distinguished speakers included [[Reid Hoffman]], a Marshall Scholar, and [[David Reitze]], Director of LIGO Laboratory. The forum highlighted societal challenges and opportunities raised by explosive innovations in these fields as they interact with advances in machine learning, artificial intelligence, and data science.

In 2019, the association hosted the Marshall Forum with the [[Carnegie Endowment for International Peace]], focusing on peace and prosperity. The Forum featured 17 speakers including the Governor of the Bank of England [[Mark Carney]], the Director of U.S. National Security Agency General [[Paul Nakasone]], former [[U.S. ambassadors]] [[Michael Froman]], [[Carla Hills]], and [[William J. Burns (diplomat)|William J. Burns]], and former [[British Ambassador to the United States]] [[Kim Darroch]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/6845a846-66b7-11e9-a79d-04f350474d62|title=Financial Times April 25, 2018, ''Even US anglophiles warn the UK over trade talks''|newspaper=Financial Times|date=April 25, 2019|last1=Giles|first1=Chris}}</ref>
